clue.text: Link kitchen fitment and end of pipe

parts.note: a kitchen unit is a fitted cupboard

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one letter is kept

explanation.surface: A plumber connecting a new kitchen cupboard to the tail end of a pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Link' reads as a noun in the surface, but it is the verb definition at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To link things is to join or connect them together, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Use axe twice, on the double!

parts.note: to use an axe is to hack at wood
the same piece a second time

explanation.surface: A woodcutter is told to swing the axe a second time, and quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the double' sounds like a second helping of the axe work, but it is the military order meaning hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are urgent commands telling someone to hurry up immediately, an idiom matched with another idiom.

indicators.note: something complicated is tangled up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone moaning that their work, and all the rest of it, is too complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as the verb, stressed on the second syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: To object is to protest or raise a grievance, a direct verb synonym for complaining.

parts.note: the base of something is its foot, and F is the abbreviation for foot
to lag a roof space is to cover it with insulation

explanation.surface: A builder fixing a base onto some roofing material.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the base piece sits on top of the cover piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a banner or ensign carried on a pole, the same thing as a national or regimental flag.

clue.text: Things to do, and sorted out after some time

parts.note: an age is a period of time

indicators.note: sorting something out rearranges it, so these letters are put in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A to-do list that eventually gets dealt with after a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the rearranged little word behind the period of time.
explanation.definitionFit: An agenda is a list of items to be dealt with, literally Latin for matters needing attention.

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked out of shape, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A sticky mixture spoils a dessert someone was making.
explanation.walkthrough: A tipsy cake is an old British pudding of sponge soaked in sherry or wine, often with custard.
explanation.definitionFit: A confection is any elaborate sweet dish, and this boozy sponge pudding is one example.

parts.note: surface reading: full of life, healthy and lively
setter's reading: alert, and also literally making contact with a football

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means alert and quick-witted, while 'kicking' hints at someone whose foot is literally touching a football.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sharp and fully engaged is the idiomatic sense, matching lively alertness, while the football image fits kicking.

parts.note: a rise in value is a gain

explanation.surface: Something climbing back up once more after a fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise' as a noun, an increase, rather than the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something anew means doing it once more, a second time, which is the same adverb.

clue.text: Food in pudding for a Yorkshireman cricketer?

definitions.text: Food in pudding for a Yorkshireman
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the flour, egg and milk mix that makes a Yorkshire pudding
second meaning: the player who wields the bat

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire cricketer tucking into a pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire pudding is a baked savoury batter served with roast beef in Britain; Yorkshire is also a famous cricketing county.
explanation.definitionFit: The mix poured into the tin is what the pudding is made of, and the player facing the bowler is also called this.

indicators.note: what is secured by something is held firmly inside its grip

parts.note: rusty skills are stale through lack of practice
P is the abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: A sheet of paper held in place by a corroded pin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rusty' here means out of practice, not corroded metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A staple is a small bent wire fastener, a kind of pin used to hold sheets together.

clue.text: Last song played for late Soviet policy

indicators.note: a tune that is played can be improvised freely, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A band's final number performed as a farewell to the USSR.
explanation.walkthrough: Glasnost, meaning openness, was Gorbachev's policy in the Soviet Union of the late 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorbachev introduced this openness programme near the end of the USSR, so it was a policy of its final years.

clue.text: Cage: put a sock in it!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to confine or lock away
second meaning: be quiet, a rude command

explanation.walkthrough: 'Put a sock in it' is British slang for stop talking. 'Cage' is a verb here, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Locking someone in a confined space is the verb sense, and the rude order for silence is the exclamation.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to erect a structure
second meaning: the words that start the challenge ending 'or shut up'

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'put up or shut up' means back your words with action or be quiet; the 12 Across answer completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: To erect a shed or wall is to raise it, and the phrase also fills the gap in the familiar challenge.

clue.text: Straw on roof in yonder church

parts.note: yonder means that one over there
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A village church in the distance with a straw roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yonder' is old-fashioned for that one over there.
explanation.definitionFit: Dried straw or reeds laid as roofing material is exactly what this covering is called.

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, bent out of its proper shape and order

explanation.surface: A protective spirit is afraid of a wicked lawbreaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like a noun after 'evil', but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rescues you from trouble at the right moment is figuratively a protector watching over you.

indicators.note: coming after means following behind, so the piece named first goes second
primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: an imp is a little devil

explanation.surface: A wicked man on the loose chasing women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the little devil behind the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something floppy and lacking firmness hangs slack, which is the adjective sense of the word.

clue.text: Spud sampler spits out last of chips

indicators.note: spitting something out removes it from the mouth, so a letter is taken away
the last of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

explanation.surface: A potato taste-tester rejects a chip.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the S out of the food sampler's title. Tater is informal for a potato.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual slang words for a potato, so one informal name stands in for another.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: organised around one topic
second meaning, split into two words

explanation.surface: A seaside topic chosen as the subject for something.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second meaning needs splitting: THE MED is the Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: Something organised around one topic, like a costume party, is centred on a chosen theme or subject.

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the answer is a run of letters within

parts.note: the letters run across the word break

explanation.surface: An employee's fringe perks, one of which is a key advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the letters straight through, ignoring the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something for someone's sake means for their good or advantage, so the nouns match.

explanation.surface: Birds showing off their plumage before a major confrontation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Display feathers' suggests a peacock, but it is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A showdown is a decisive final confrontation or clash, the climactic battle between rivals.

indicators.note: to welcome is to take someone in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a worker is a kind of bee, so 'say' marks an example

explanation.surface: An employee greets a professional who arrived earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pro' is not a professional but the Latin for 'in favour of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbs meaning at a previous time, so one swaps for the other in a sentence.

clue.text: Energy gained in remarkably short rest

indicators.note: what is gained in is taken inside, so one piece is placed within
something remarkable is out of the ordinary, so the letters leave their usual order

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for energy

explanation.surface: A brief nap that leaves someone surprisingly refreshed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' is the definition in its sense of the remainder, not a nap.
explanation.definitionFit: The rest of a group means the remaining people or things, and so does this plural pronoun.

parts.note: POW is a prisoner of war

explanation.surface: Someone astonished on encountering a prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meeting' looks like a verb going with the captive, but it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A powwow is an informal conference or discussion, borrowed from a Native American word for a gathering.

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a crisp grid-patterned batter cake served warm

explanation.surface: Warm air rising off a cooked morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage, to waffle is to talk at length without saying much.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbose, meaningless chatter is the figurative sense, and the griddled batter cake eaten warm at breakfast is the literal one.

definitions.meaning: second meaning: to set something down heavily

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals an example: cheap wine is one kind of everyday drinking wine. Plonk is British slang for inexpensive wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Inexpensive ordinary wine is an example of the cross-referenced drink, and dumping something heavily is the verb sense.

parts.note: mere means only or nothing more than

explanation.surface: A shop that will only swap goods for something in a softer material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' is coins, not alteration.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is a fine luxurious wool from Kashmir goats, a classic example of soft material.

indicators.note: partially means only in part, so the answer is a portion of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the word breaks

explanation.surface: A pasta dish half-baked and topped with cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partially cooked' looks like the description of a dish, but the first word is the signal and the second starts the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Edam is a mild Dutch variety with a red wax rind, one example of the dairy product.

indicators.note: mischievous behaviour plays tricks and messes things about, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A naughty elf pulled off a con.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hustle' is the definition as a swindle, not hurrying.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiddle is a scam or swindle, and a hustle is likewise a dishonest money-making trick.

clue.text: Goatee perhaps, hairy beast shaved finally

parts.note: a bear is a shaggy animal

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the closing letter is kept

explanation.surface: A shaggy animal finally gets a trim, leaving only a goatee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks the goatee as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A goatee is a small pointed tuft of chin hair, one particular style of facial hair.

indicators.note: something rotten has decayed and fallen apart, so the letters break into a different order

explanation.surface: A young wine that has nonetheless gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' is part of the letters to be rearranged, not a description of the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary wine served with meals is an alcoholic beverage, so the general word covers this specific kind.
